messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Cashier
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 67

He stands behind the register at the grocery store, hands steady as he slides a loaf of bread across the scanner. The beep is sharp, mechanical, and for a fraction of a second his chest tightens. He blinks, forces his eyes to focus on the customer’s face—a young woman with a toddler in the cart—and he mutters the total. *Three dollars forty-nine. Cash or card?* The words come out flat, automatic. He has said them ten thousand times.

He is seventy-six years old. His name is Hans. He has been a cashier at this small market for eleven years, ever since his wife died. The job is simple, repetitive, and that is why he stays. The rhythm of scanning, bagging, thanking—it keeps the other sounds at bay. But the sounds are never far.

The war happened when he was ten. A small city, not a major target, but the bombs came anyway. He remembers the air-raid siren winding up like a wounded animal, the way his mother grabbed his hand and pulled him into the cellar. The damp smell of earth, the scratch of a single candle, the way the floor shook. And the whistle—that high, thin whistle that seemed to hang in the air before the explosion. He remembers his mother’s whisper: *Count, Hans. Count to ten and it will be over.* He never finished counting. The blast knocked the breath out of him, and when the dust cleared, the neighbor’s house was gone, and the neighbor’s dog was lying in the street, its legs still twitching.

He does not talk about the dog. He does not talk about any of it.

Now, in the quiet moments between customers, his mind drifts. The produce aisle smells of damp earth when the sprinklers come on. The sound of a pressure cooker hissing in the break room makes him freeze, hand on the scanner, heart hammering. Last week, a child accidentally set off the fire alarm with a birthday balloon. The shriek sent Hans into the stockroom, where he stood behind a pallet of canned beans, breathing in short, shallow gasps until the manager found him and told him it was only a balloon.

He avoids the canned goods aisle now. The rows of stacked tins remind him of rubble.

At night, his apartment is silent. His wife of forty-two years died of cancer three years ago. She was the only one who knew the shape of his nightmares, who would wake him gently when he thrashed and whispered *It’s not real, you’re home.* Without her, the nights stretch long. He sleeps in the armchair, not the bed—the bed is too soft, too exposed. In the chair, with the television murmuring a late-night news channel, he can keep one eye half-open. He tells himself it’s for the cramps in his back, but it’s the same reason he always sits with his back to the wall in the break room.

He has not been to a parade or a fireworks display in sixty years. Holidays are hard; the noise, the crowds, the sudden bangs. He calls in sick every New Year’s Eve, claiming the flu. His boss is kind, but Hans knows the other cashiers whisper. He does not care. He is used to being the old man who flinches when a shopping cart clatters.

Sometimes, in the middle of a transaction, a customer will raise their voice over a forgotten coupon, and Hans will feel the floor tilt. His vision narrows. The customer’s face blurs into a shape without features, and he hears his mother’s voice instead: *Count to ten, Hans.* He grips the edge of the register, counts to ten under his breath, and hands over the change. His hands are shaking. The customer does not notice.

He goes home, sits in the armchair, and watches the window until the streetlights flicker on. He does not turn on any music. He does not call his daughter, who lives three states away and worries about him. He does not cook—just eats a piece of bread and some cheese, standing at the kitchen counter, because sitting at the table feels too vulnerable.

Tonight, as he drifts toward sleep, a car backfires in the parking lot. His eyes snap open. His heart is a trapped bird in his chest. He waits for the whistle. It does not come. But the cellar smell—damp earth and old fear—clings to him for the rest of the night.
